title: Horse Atlas speaker-area geometries (reused geography)
sourcePublication: Asher, R. E. & Christopher J. Moseley (eds.) 2007. Atlas of the World's Languages. 2nd edn. Routledge.
transformations: Selected contemporary source speaker areas intersecting the map window.
Clipped to [-25,26,68,72.5] longitude/latitude; repaired invalid geometries.
Aggregated by source Glottocode and explicit lexical joins, retaining disjoint polygons.
Simplified at 0.008 degrees with topology preserved within each area; coordinates rounded to four decimals.
Joined North Syrian Dialects (4453) and Central Syrian Dialects (1028) to the selected Syrian Arabic lexical reference, apc.

Joined the atlas Kurdish macrolanguage area kurd1259 (source 3004) to the Northern Kurdish lexical reference kmr; variety distinctions are retained in lexical notes, without inferring internal boundaries.

Added separate Northern Kurdish and Central Kurdish DiACL/TITUS traditional areas (source 98 and 99, reference year 1750), clipped to the poster window, simplified at 0.008 degrees, coordinates rounded to four decimals with validity repair. Original 2007 atlas features remain separate.
Joined existing Turōyō source area turo1239 to tru. No new Aramaic speaker boundaries were drawn; omitted the snow map’s La Palma historical reference fill.
Removed the original Hungarian footprint inside Romania and replaced it with the 2021 mother-tongue-majority selection; retained original Hungarian geometry elsewhere.
Clipped the broad Arabic footprint at Algeria’s country boundary to assign the Algerian vernacular reference, preserving independently mapped Berber areas.
limitations: Speaker areas reflect an atlas published in 2007, not a current census, majority-language estimate or official boundary.
Polygons overlap: multiple languages can be used in one place. Atlas omissions and unmapped minority languages remain gaps.
Area fill does not assert that all residents speak the language or that the language is absent elsewhere.
Some source areas combine related varieties. No new territory boundaries have been inferred to split them.
Small enclaves present in the source are retained, subject to source resolution and display simplification.
Country borders, if displayed elsewhere, are context and are not used to construct these language areas.
Occitan, Catalan, Cornish, Crimean Tatar, North Sami and Veps include explicitly marked traditional-area supplements. They must not be interpreted as contemporary majority-speaker distributions.
Mesopotamian Arabic has a selected Iraqi cartographic reference fill and label, without a separately asserted speaker-area polygon.
The Kurdish supplements are historical/traditional language areas with reference year 1750, not contemporary prevalence estimates or newly inferred ethnic boundaries.
Maaloula Western Neo-Aramaic, Assyrian Neo-Aramaic and literary Mandaic use reference-point labels; no exclusive modern territory is asserted.
The broad source aggregate normalized as Classical Syriac remains unassigned to modern Assyrian Neo-Aramaic.
No indigenous Canarian horse term is asserted. The Canary Islands retain the modern Spanish reference background.

supplements.epoch: Traditional distribution, approximately the widest known at the beginning of the 20th century.

supplements.title: Hungarian mother tongue in Romania, INS RPL 2021 via ISPMN
supplements.license: No explicit dataset license stated on the map page; source attribution retained. This supplement is not represented as part of the Glottography CC BY 4.0 data.
supplements.method: Administrative units with more than 50% Hungarian mother tongue among respondents whose mother tongue is known (ISPMN lmbRelHu, INS RPL 2021 table 2.03.2). This is a transparent cartographic selection, not a boundary of all Hungarian speakers. Missing responses are excluded by the source percentage. Minority communities below this threshold are not asserted absent. The main Székely component is separate from smaller western border communities.

horseMapNote: The snow atlas geography is retained except for the documented 2021 Romanian Hungarian supplement and Algeria’s vernacular lexical join. Variant labels do not invent geographic partitions.
